tts: Hennessy is the best-selling cognac in the world. Last year, LVMH sold around seventy-five million bottles of cognac, and almost all of them carried one name. But here's the strange part: the most famous French brandy was started by an Irishman, its biggest market is not France but the United States, and its loyal fans were built, decade by decade, by people the luxury world ignored. So how did a soldier from County Cork end up with his name on a bottle in a Tupac song? Along the way, we'll meet an insect that almost wiped out cognac, a king who inspired a famous label, and the real reason there's an H in LVMH. Let's pour this story slowly.

Richard Hennessy was born in Ireland in seventeen twenty-four. Like many Irish Catholics of his time, he left home to serve in the army of the French king, Louis the Fifteenth, in the famous Irish Brigade. While stationed near the Charente region in western France, he discovered the local brandy. He sent barrels of it home to his family and friends in Ireland, and the orders kept coming. So he stayed. In seventeen sixty-five, in the small riverside town of Cognac, he started his own trading house. The brand still counts its birthday from that year. His son James grew the business, shipped cognac across Europe, and even sat in the French parliament. The company's official name is still Jas Hennessy and Company, after him.

So what actually is cognac? Like champagne, the name is protected: it can only come from this region. The best area is called Grande Champagne, which has nothing to do with bubbles. The word comes from its chalky soil. It's brandy made from white grapes, grown only in a protected region around the town. The wine is distilled twice in copper pot stills, then aged in French oak barrels for years. While it ages, a little of it evaporates through the wood, about two percent every year. The locals call it the angels' share. And the blackened walls of the town's cellars are covered in a fungus that feeds on those vapours. Age is everything: V.S. must be aged at least two years, V.S.O.P. at least four, and X.O. at least ten.

And the Hennessy family helped invent that ladder. According to the house, in eighteen seventeen, the future King George the Fourth of Britain asked for a very superior old pale cognac. That request gave us V.S.O.P. In the eighteen-sixties, Maurice Hennessy began marking quality with stars on the label, a system other houses soon copied. And in eighteen seventy, he created X.O., extra old, a blend first made for family and friends. Then disaster hit: a tiny insect called phylloxera arrived from America and destroyed most of the vineyards of Cognac. The region had to be replanted almost from scratch.

Through all of this, one thing stayed the same: the taste. Since eighteen-oh-six, the job of master blender at Hennessy has been passed down inside one family, the Fillioux. The current master blender, Renaud Fillioux de Gironde, is the eighth generation. Every morning, a small tasting committee meets to sample eaux-de-vie, the young brandies that will one day be blended. The house also keeps a library of very old eaux-de-vie, some from the nineteenth century, resting in glass jars once the wood has given all it can. Some of the spirits in the cellars are older than anyone alive. A blend you buy today may contain brandies chosen by people who died long ago, for a future they would never see.

Now, the American chapter. During the world wars, Black American soldiers were stationed in France, and many tasted cognac there for the first time. After the war, most luxury brands refused to market to Black customers. Hennessy did the opposite. By the nineteen-fifties, it was advertising in Ebony and Jet, magazines made for Black readers, using Black models. And in nineteen sixty-three, it hired Herb Douglas, an Olympic bronze medalist in the long jump, and made him a vice president, one of the first Black executives at a major American company. That kind of respect is remembered for generations. The brand even supported a documentary about this relationship, called An Unexpected History.

So when hip-hop arrived, cognac was already part of the culture. In the nineties and two-thousands, rappers turned Henny into a lyric, a symbol of success you could actually afford for one night. Tupac even recorded a song simply called Hennessy. When Busta Rhymes released Pass the Courvoisier, sales of that rival cognac reportedly jumped. Other brands copied the playbook, but Hennessy had a head start of decades. And it leaned in: limited bottles designed by street artists, and later a partnership with the N.B.A. Today, the United States is Hennessy's biggest market, with around three million cases a year.

Meanwhile, the company itself became part of something much bigger. In nineteen seventy-one, Hennessy merged with Moët et Chandon, the champagne house, to form Moët Hennessy. In nineteen eighty-seven, Moët Hennessy merged with Louis Vuitton. That's where the letters come from: L.V.M.H. stands for Louis Vuitton, Moët, Hennessy. Soon after, Bernard Arnault took control of the group and built a fashion empire, but cognac stayed one of its most profitable businesses for years. The British drinks giant Diageo still owns about a third of Moët Hennessy. So a brandy business started by an Irish soldier is now part of the largest luxury group on Earth, next to handbags, watches and perfume.

But even the king of cognac can stumble. Cognac sales boomed during the pandemic, and then the party ended. In twenty twenty-four, China put special duties on European brandy, in a trade fight over electric cars. In twenty twenty-five, the United States added a fifteen percent tariff on European spirits. Hit from both sides, Moët Hennessy's cognac sales fell about twelve percent last year, and U.S. shipments of Hennessy dropped too. The company is now trying new things, like ready-to-drink cocktails, to win back younger drinkers who buy less spirits than their parents. And cognac is a slow business: brandy distilled today won't be sold for years. So when demand drops, warehouses fill up, and some growers in the region have started pulling up their vines.

So, look at the whole journey. An Irish soldier far from home. A small town by a river. A family of tasters passing down one palate for two hundred years. A brand that respected customers others ignored, and was rewarded with loyalty that outlived generations. Hennessy's story isn't really about brandy. It's about time: years in a barrel, generations in a cellar, and decades of trust. And next time you see a bottle with a small arm holding an axe on the label, you'll know: that's the Hennessy family's Irish coat of arms. And that's something even tariffs can't evaporate overnight.
